title: The definition of a liability: obligation, transfer and past events
summary: The three criteria that must all hold for a liability: an obligation, to transfer an economic resource, that is present and from past events.

chunks.heading: The liability definition and its three criteria
chunks.explanation_md:
A **liability** is a **present obligation** of the entity **to transfer an economic resource** as a result of **past events**.

For a liability to exist, **all three** criteria must be met:

1. The entity **has an obligation**.
2. The obligation is **to transfer an economic resource**.
3. The obligation is a **present obligation** that exists **as a result of past events**.

The next chunks take each criterion in turn.

key_terms.meaning: A present obligation of the entity to transfer an economic resource as a result of past events.

chunks.exam_line: A liability needs all three: an obligation, to transfer an economic resource, that is a present obligation arising from past events.

chunks.heading: Criterion 1: an obligation
chunks.explanation_md:
An **obligation** is a **duty or responsibility the entity has no practical ability to avoid**. It is **always owed to another party** (a person, entity, group or society at large). You need not know **who** it is owed to.

- If one party has an obligation to transfer a resource, another has a **right** to receive it. But one party recognising a liability at an amount does **not** mean the other must recognise an asset at the same amount; Standards may differ for relevance reasons.
- Obligations come from **contract, legislation** or similar and are usually legally enforceable. They can also come from **customary practices, published policies or specific statements** if the entity has no practical ability to act inconsistently. These are sometimes called **constructive obligations**.
- A duty can be **conditional on a future action the entity itself may take** (for example operating in a particular market on a future date). It is an obligation if the entity has **no practical ability to avoid** that action.
- Preparing statements on a **going concern** basis implies no practical ability to avoid a transfer that could be avoided only by liquidating or ceasing trading.
- It can be a close call: no practical ability to avoid may mean that avoiding it would have **economic consequences significantly more adverse** than the transfer. But **neither an intention to make the transfer, nor a high likelihood of it, is enough** to conclude there is no practical ability to avoid it.
- If it is **uncertain whether an obligation exists** (for example a compensation claim for alleged wrongdoing), it is uncertain whether a liability exists until resolved, for example by a court.

key_terms.meaning: A duty or responsibility that an entity has no practical ability to avoid.
An obligation arising from an entity's customary practices, published policies or specific statements when it cannot practically act otherwise.

chunks.exam_line: An obligation is a duty the entity has no practical ability to avoid; it is owed to another party, and may arise from contract, law or constructive practices. Intention or likelihood of payment is not enough.

chunks.heading: Criterion 2: a transfer of an economic resource
chunks.explanation_md:
The obligation must have the **potential to require the entity to transfer an economic resource** to another party. It need **not be certain, or even likely**, that a transfer will be required. For example, it may be required only **if a specified uncertain future event occurs**. It is enough that the obligation **already exists** and in **at least one circumstance** would require a transfer.

So an obligation can be a liability even if the **probability of a transfer is low**. That low probability may affect **what information is provided and how**, including whether the liability is **recognised** and how it is **measured**.

Obligations to transfer an economic resource include: **paying cash**; **delivering goods or providing services**; **exchanging resources on unfavourable terms** (for example a forward contract to sell on currently unfavourable terms, or an option that lets another party buy from the entity); a transfer **if a specified uncertain event occurs**; and issuing a financial instrument that will oblige the entity to transfer a resource.

**Ways out.** Instead of fulfilling the obligation to the party owed, an entity may **negotiate a release**, **transfer the obligation to a third party**, or **replace it with another obligation** through a new transaction. The entity has the obligation **until it has settled, transferred or replaced it**.
chunks.exam_line: An obligation to transfer need not be certain or likely; a low probability can still leave a liability. Examples: pay cash, deliver goods or services, exchange on unfavourable terms.

chunks.heading: Criterion 3: a present obligation from past events
chunks.explanation_md:
A present obligation exists as a result of past events **only if**:

(a) the entity has **already obtained economic benefits or taken an action**; **and**
(b) as a consequence, it **will or may have to transfer a resource it would not otherwise have had to transfer**.

Benefits obtained could be goods or services. The action taken could be operating a particular business or operating in a particular market. If the benefits are obtained or the action taken **over time**, the obligation may **accumulate** over that time.

- **New legislation**: a present obligation arises only when, because of obtaining benefits or taking an action to which it applies, the entity will or may have to transfer a resource. **Enactment alone is not enough.** The same goes for customary practices, policies or statements.
- A present obligation can exist even if the transfer **cannot be enforced until a future date**. For example, a contractual liability to pay cash may exist now though payment is due later.
- **Example: salary.** If an entity has a contract to pay an employee a salary in exchange for services, it has **no present obligation to pay the salary until it has received the services**. Before then the contract is an **executory contract**: a combined right and obligation to exchange future salary for future services.
chunks.exam_line: A present obligation from past events requires that the entity has already obtained benefits or taken an action, and as a result may have to transfer a resource it otherwise would not. Salary is owed only after the services are received.

questions.stem: Explain why a salary contract does not give rise to a liability until the employee's services are received.
questions.model_answer_md:
A **present obligation from past events** exists only if the entity has already obtained **economic benefits or taken an action** and as a result may have to transfer a resource it would not otherwise have had to transfer.

Under a contract to pay a salary in exchange for services, the entity has not yet obtained any benefit until it has **received the employee's services**. So it has **no present obligation to pay** the salary yet.

Before then the contract is an **executory contract**: a combined right and obligation to exchange future salary for future employee services.

questions.stem: Discuss the definition of a liability with respect to its three criteria.
questions.model_answer_md:
A **liability** is a **present obligation of the entity to transfer an economic resource as a result of past events**. All three criteria must be satisfied.

**1. Obligation.** A duty or responsibility the entity has **no practical ability to avoid**, always owed to another party. It may come from contract, legislation or similar, or from **customary practices, published policies or specific statements** (constructive obligations). It can depend on a future action of the entity if the entity has no practical ability to avoid taking it. A going concern basis implies no practical ability to avoid transfers that could be avoided only by liquidating or ceasing to trade. Neither an **intention** to transfer nor a **high likelihood** of transfer is enough. If it is uncertain whether an obligation exists (for example a compensation claim) it is uncertain whether a liability exists until resolved.

**2. Transfer of an economic resource.** The obligation must have the **potential** to require a transfer. It need not be certain or likely; it may depend on an uncertain future event. A low probability can still leave a liability but may affect information and recognition. Examples: paying cash, delivering goods or providing services, exchanging resources on unfavourable terms. The entity can settle, transfer to a third party, or replace the obligation, and has it until it does so.

**3. Present obligation from past events.** The entity must already have **obtained economic benefits or taken an action**, and as a result may have to transfer something it would not otherwise have. Enactment of legislation alone is not enough. An obligation can exist even if it cannot be enforced until later. Example: salary is not owed until the employee's services are received.

questions.stem: Explain, using the Framework, when a present obligation exists where new legislation is enacted or an entity has customary practices.
questions.model_answer_md:
A present obligation exists as a result of past events **only if** the entity has **already obtained economic benefits or taken an action** and as a consequence will or may have to transfer a resource it would not otherwise have had to transfer.

**New legislation.** A present obligation arises only when, as a consequence of obtaining benefits or taking an action to which the legislation applies, the entity will or may have to transfer a resource. **The enactment of legislation alone is not enough.**

**Customary practices, published policies or specific statements** (constructive obligations) work the same way: they give rise to a present obligation only when the entity has obtained benefits or taken an action to which the practice, policy or statement applies and may have to transfer a resource it would not otherwise have.

**Over time.** If benefits are obtained or actions taken over time, the obligation may accumulate over that time.

**Timing of payment.** A present obligation can exist even if the transfer cannot be enforced until a future date, such as a contractual liability to pay cash on a later date.

rubric.point: Benefits obtained or action taken, and transfer it would not otherwise make
Legislation: enactment alone not enough
Constructive obligations follow the same test
Obligation may build up over time and can exist before it is enforceable
